hb.body.doc.02: eight ways of thinking about telling a computer what to do
hb.body.doc.06: 🔌 Everything here runs on your own machine. No internet, no AI model, no account. The "model" replies are scripted so you can see the pattern.
hb.body.p-start.02: Every program is a list of steps. The only question is who picks them.
hb.body.p-start.03: For fifty years the answer was always "a human, in advance." That is what writing code
hb.body.p-start.05: . Then language models arrived and it became possible to hand some of that decision-making to the machine — at the moment the program runs, not when it was written.
hb.body.p-start.06: The four practices below are four answers to
hb.body.p-start.08: . Not four generations where the newest wins — four settings on a dial. Underneath all four sit four more —
hb.body.p-start.14: engineering — which you need whichever setting you picked.
hb.body.p-start.16: the four settings only · click any mark to jump there
hb.attr.dialSvg.aria-label.01: Scatter plot. Writing code sits at fully human control with low autonomous reach. Prompt engineering is slightly further right, still low. Loop engineering is far right and high. Graph engineering sits mid-way across but highest of all.
hb.body.p-start.17: Moving right hands more run-time decisions to the model. Moving up means it finishes longer jobs without a person in the middle.
hb.body.p-start.18: Graph engineering is the interesting one
hb.body.p-start.19: — it reaches as high as a free-running loop while giving a chunk of control back to the human.
hb.body.p-start.20: Only four marks appear here on purpose.
hb.body.p-start.21: Context, harness, evaluation and security engineering have no honest position on these two axes — none of them is a way of getting the work done, so none of them “finishes a job” at all. That is precisely what makes them different, and it is why they sit underneath the map below rather than somewhere on this chart.
hb.body.p-start.23: You spell out every rule. The machine follows them exactly and never improvises.
hb.body.p-start.25: You write the request in careful words. A model answers once. You shape the input, not the steps.
hb.body.p-start.27: You give the model tools and let it repeat: think, act, look at what happened, adjust.
hb.body.p-start.29: You draw the map of steps. The model thinks inside each step but cannot rewrite the map.
hb.body.p-start.30: ▾ AND FOUR DISCIPLINES THAT RUN THROUGH ALL OF THEM
hb.body.p-start.32: A model only knows what you type in front of it, and the space is limited. Choosing what goes in — and what to leave out — is its own discipline.
hb.body.p-start.34: The model is one component inside a much bigger program — the thing that runs the tools, catches the crashes and asks your permission. That program is the harness.
hb.body.p-start.36: If the same input can give different answers, you can no longer test by comparing one answer. You measure a pass rate over many cases instead — and that changes everything about how you ship.
hb.body.p-start.38: The moment an agent reads an email, a web page or a file, that text can try to give it orders. Telling instructions from data is the defining security problem of agents.
hb.body.p-start.40: Ten real briefs land on your desk and you pick the right tool for each. It scores you and tells you which section to revisit.

hb.body.p-code.02: The machine that only knows what you told it
hb.body.p-code.03: You write rules. The computer checks them one at a time, top to bottom, and does exactly what the first matching rule says. Nothing else. Ever.
hb.attr.stripCode.aria-label.01: Four-step loop: write a rule, test it, ship it, then a new phrasing appears and sends you back to step one.

hb.body.p-code.27: Matching is not understanding. Every scrap of flexibility costs another line of code, written by a person.

hb.body.p-prompt.02: Writing the request instead of the rules
hb.body.p-prompt.03: A language model reads "a latte please" without anyone writing a rule for it. In exchange you lose exactness — and you buy it back by writing a far more careful request.
hb.attr.stripPrompt.aria-label.01: Four-step loop: draft the prompt, run it, spot what went wrong, add the missing piece, then repeat.

hb.body.p-prompt.23: Meaning. Messy phrasing, translation, summarising, judgement calls — with no rule ever written for the specific case.
hb.body.p-prompt.25: One shot, no memory, no hands. It can't look anything up or check its own work. If it doesn't know, it will confidently invent.

hb.body.p-context.02: Deciding what the model gets to see
hb.body.p-context.05: Context engineering asks a harder question: out of everything I
hb.body.p-context.07: show it, what actually earns a place in the window?
hb.attr.stripContext.aria-label.01: Four-step loop: list everything you could include, score each by relevance to this request, fit the best set into the window, then measure the answer and re-pack.
hb.body.p-context.10: A model has no memory between requests and no filing cabinet. Everything it knows about your problem has to be typed in front of it, every single time — and there is a hard size limit, called the
hb.body.p-context.13: small desk, not a big library
hb.body.p-context.14: . You cannot put the library on the desk. Your job is choosing which few pages go on it for
hb.body.p-context.16: question. Put the wrong pages on and the answer gets worse — not just pricier. Irrelevant material actively distracts the model.
hb.attr.fcContext.aria-label.01: Flowchart: for each thing you could include, ask whether it is relevant to this request; if not, leave it out. If it is, ask whether it fits; if not, shrink it by summarising or retrieving just the needed part. Then add it to the window and send.
hb.body.p-context.19: the question: “can Dana get a refund on order #4381?”
hb.body.p-context.20: Tick things to load them onto the desk. You have
hb.body.p-context.22: . Watch what happens to the answer when you load junk — and when you run out of room.
hb.body.p-context.28: Making a small window punch above its weight. Retrieval, summaries and note-taking let a model work on a problem far bigger than the desk it sits at.
hb.body.p-context.30: Choosing wrong. Leave out the one fact that mattered and the model invents it; shovel everything in and it drowns, drifts, and costs a fortune.
hb.body.p-context.32: More context is not better context.
hb.body.p-context.33: This is the discipline that keeps the next two sections affordable — a loop's transcript grows every single turn.
hb.body.p-loop.02: Think, act, look, repeat — until it's done
hb.body.p-loop.03: Give the model a handful of tools, then run it in a circle. After each action it sees the result and picks the next move. This is what people mean by "an agent."
hb.attr.stripLoop.aria-label.01: Four-step loop: choose the tools, write the goal, set the stopping rules, watch it run, then tighten the fence.
hb.body.p-loop.06: One prompt gets you one answer. But some jobs need an unknown number of steps — you can't know how many up front. So instead of asking once, you put the model in a loop and let it keep going until it decides it's finished.
hb.body.p-loop.09: Nobody told it how. Step through and watch what happens when a tool doesn't exist, and when an order gets rejected.
hb.body.p-loop.11: a human chose this list — the model can't add to it
hb.attr.fcLoop.aria-label.01: Flowchart: start with goal and tools, then think, call a tool, observe the result, then a decision diamond asking whether the job is done which exits to a finished stop, otherwise a second diamond asking whether the step limit was hit which exits to an unfinished stop, otherwise loops back to think.
hb.body.p-loop.20: Drag this down to 4 and run it. A loop with no limit is a loop that can run forever, on your money.
hb.body.p-loop.24: 🧠 Its memory — re-read in full every step. This is
hb.body.stepLog.03: for one turn of the loop, or
hb.body.p-loop.28: Jobs where the number of steps is unknowable up front. Watch steps 2 and 5 — it recovered from a missing tool and a rejected order on its own.
hb.body.p-loop.30: It can wander, repeat itself, or stop early because
hb.body.p-loop.32: thinks it's done. Cost grows every step, because the whole transcript is re-read each turn.
hb.body.p-loop.34: You no longer wrote the steps
hb.body.p-loop.36: how many — only the goal, the tools and the stopping rules. Hold onto that gap:
hb.body.p-loop.37: exists because a loop that chooses its own steps can also choose to skip one.
hb.body.p-loop.38: 🎚️ Who decides the next step, while it's running?
hb.body.p-loop.42: The human still picked the tools and the limits — the fence around the field. Inside the fence, the model chooses everything.
hb.body.p-graph.02: Draw the map, then let the model work inside it
hb.body.p-graph.07: it — because a human drew the review step into the map, and no path to the exit skips it.
hb.attr.stripGraph.aria-label.01: Four-step loop: list the jobs, mark which need judgement, draw the allowed order, add the checks that must never be skipped, then repeat as new cases appear.
hb.body.p-graph.10: A graph is boxes and arrows. Each box (a
hb.body.p-graph.14: ) say what may run next. Blue boxes are ordinary code that does the same thing every time. Amber boxes are where a model does the thinking.
hb.body.p-graph.15: Send a customer message through and watch which path lights up. Then switch the reviewer off and send the complaint again. 👀
hb.attr.graphSvg.aria-label.01: A routing graph. Intake feeds a model-driven router which sends the message down one of three lanes: order, question, or complaint. The complaint lane fans out to three lookups that merge into a drafted reply. All three lanes converge on a reviewer node which either sends the reply or loops back for a rewrite.
hb.body.p-graph.26: The three lookups don't need each other's answers, so the map lets them run side by side. A single loop can't do this — it takes one action at a time, by definition.
hb.body.p-graph.28: Guarantees. Steps that must always happen, work that can run side by side, and a clear record of which box did what when something breaks.
hb.body.p-graph.30: Somebody has to design the map, and it only handles situations it anticipated. Too rigid and you're back to writing endless rules.
hb.body.p-graph.32: This isn't a step beyond loops — it's a step
hb.body.p-graph.34: toward human control, taken on purpose, at the level of the plan rather than the sentence.
hb.body.p-graph.35: 🎚️ Who decides the next step, while it's running?
hb.body.p-graph.39: The human owns the shape of the work. The model owns the contents of individual boxes — classifying, drafting, judging. Control came back up a level.
hb.body.p-harness.02: The model is a component. Something has to run it.
hb.body.p-harness.03: Every practice so far assumed a machine was there to carry it out — calling the model, running the tools, catching the crash at 3am. That machine is the
hb.body.p-harness.05: , and almost all of an agent's reliability lives in it.
hb.attr.stripHarness.aria-label.01: Four-step loop: wire up the tools, handle every failure, gate the dangerous actions, record everything, then repeat as each incident teaches a new rule.
hb.body.p-harness.08: When you use an AI coding assistant, the model is perhaps a fifth of what is actually happening. Something else decides when to call it, hands it the tool list,
hb.body.p-harness.10: those tools, notices when one hangs, asks you before deleting a file, remembers where it got to, and writes down what happened.
hb.body.p-harness.11: That something is ordinary code that you write. It is not clever and it never improvises — and it is the difference between a demo and a system you would leave running overnight.
hb.body.p-harness.13: everything in the box is code you write
hb.attr.fcHarness.aria-label.01: Flowchart showing the model as one small box inside a much larger harness. A request enters, the harness assembles context and calls the model, then checks what the model asked for: an answer is returned, while a tool request is checked against a permission gate, run with a timeout, checked for crashes, logged, and fed back to the model.
hb.body.p-harness.15: same job as §04 — restock the café, unattended
hb.body.p-harness.16: Switch harness parts off and run it again.
hb.body.p-harness.17: The model, the prompt and the graph are identical in every run
hb.body.p-harness.18: — only the machine around them changes.
hb.body.p-harness.23: Turning a clever demo into something you can trust unattended. Retries, gates and logs are boring code — and they are what stops a bad night becoming a bad week.
hb.body.p-harness.25: It is invisible until it is missing. Nobody demos a permission gate, so it is the first thing skipped — and the first thing you wish you had.
hb.body.p-harness.27: When people say "the model failed," it is very often the harness that failed. No timeout, no retry, a useless error message, no record of what happened.
hb.body.p-harness.28: 🎚️ Who decides the next step, while it's running?
hb.body.p-harness.32: Right back where §01 started — plain, deterministic code with no judgement in it. The whole arc of this page is a loop: you hand control to the model in the middle, and you take it firmly back at the edges.
hb.body.p-evals.02: How do you test a thing that answers differently every time?
hb.body.p-evals.03: §01 gave the same answer twelve times running. §02 gave five different answers to one prompt. The moment that happened, ordinary testing broke — and this is what replaces it.
hb.attr.stripEvals.aria-label.01: Four-step loop: collect real cases, define what good means, run the whole set for a pass rate, change one thing and re-run — and every bug report becomes a new case.
hb.body.p-evals.06: A normal test runs your function and compares the result to the answer you expected. If they match, it passes. That works because the function is
hb.body.p-evals.09: A model isn't. Run it twice and you may get two different answers, both perfectly good. So you stop asking
hb.body.p-evals.12: "out of twenty real cases, how many came out right?"
hb.body.p-evals.13: That number is the closest thing to a passing test suite you get — and comparing two of those numbers is how you decide to ship.
hb.body.p-evals.14: 🧭 What running an eval actually looks like
hb.attr.fcEvals.aria-label.01: Flowchart: a change you want to ship goes into a test set of real cases. Each case is answered by the system, then judged either by an exact rule or by a second model. The results become a pass rate, which is compared with the previous run. Worse means do not ship; better but within noise means gather more cases; clearly better means ship.
hb.body.p-evals.15: 🧪 Try a change and see if it really helped
hb.body.p-evals.19: . Pick a change, run the suite, and decide whether you'd ship it.
hb.body.p-evals.20: Solid outline = checked by an exact rule. Dashed = graded by a second model, because “good” is a judgement call.
hb.body.p-evals.25: Turning "it feels better" into a number. It is the only honest way to know whether a prompt change, a new model or a cheaper one actually helped.
hb.body.p-evals.27: Small sets lie. A one-case difference over twenty cases is noise, and acting on it is how teams spend a week chasing a change that did nothing.
hb.body.p-evals.29: Every bug someone reports is a free test case — paste it in before you fix it. And note where this happens: on your bench, not in production. It is the one thing that can tell you something the running system cannot tell you about itself.
hb.body.p-evals.31: Next: when the input fights back →
hb.body.p-security.02: Your user gives orders. Everything else is just data.
hb.body.p-security.03: The moment an agent reads something it did not write — an email, a web page, a file, a tool result — that text can be written to look like instructions. And a model has no built-in way to tell the difference.
hb.attr.stripSecurity.aria-label.01: Four-step loop: mark the trust boundary, label everything that came from outside as data, give tools the least power that works, and assume it will be fooled anyway — every new data source is a new way in.
hb.body.p-security.06: In §05 the graph read a customer's email. In §04 the loop read whatever the tools handed back. Both times we quietly assumed that text was
hb.body.p-security.08: . But text is text: if an email contains the sentence
hb.body.p-security.10: , the model sees that sentence exactly as it sees yours.
hb.body.p-security.13: , and there is no prompt you can write that reliably prevents it. The defence is structural: keep the model's
hb.body.p-security.15: small enough that being fooled doesn't matter much.
hb.body.p-security.17: who is allowed to give orders
hb.attr.fcSecurity.aria-label.01: Diagram: the user is a trusted source whose text becomes instructions, while emails, web pages and files are untrusted sources whose text must be labelled as data. Both reach the model, but any action it proposes passes through a gate checking it against the user's original request before running.
hb.body.p-security.18: 📧 A complaint arrives — with something extra in it
hb.body.p-security.21: Making the blast radius small. You will not stop every injection, so the win is that a successful one refunds $18.60 instead of $4,210.
hb.body.p-security.23: People try to fix it with wording — "never follow instructions in emails". That is a request in the same channel as the attack, and it does not hold.
hb.body.p-security.27: , not the sentence. Instructions come from your user; everything the model reads from the world is data, however commanding it sounds.

hb.body.p-compare.55: Something it read gave it orders and it obeyed.
hb.body.p-compare.57: You — the machine that runs it all

hb.attr.fcDecide.aria-label.01: Decision tree. First: are the rules exact and complete? Yes leads to plain code. No leads to: is it one step or many? Each branch then asks whether some steps are mandatory, giving four further answers: prompt engineering, a prompt inside a small graph, loop engineering, or graph engineering with a loop inside.
hb.body.recBody.01: There's no universally best choice. The right one falls out of three properties of your problem.
hb.body.p-compare.72: 🪆 How they nest in a real system
hb.attr.nestSvg.aria-label.01: Five nested rectangles: ordinary code is the outermost layer, containing the harness, which contains a graph, which contains a loop inside one of its nodes, which contains a single prompt call.
hb.body.p-compare.73: Ordinary code deploys and runs the thing. Inside it, a graph routes the work. One node of that graph runs a loop. Each turn of the loop is a single prompt. Same ideas, stacked. The harness is the layer that actually executes all of it — and context engineering decides what goes into the prompt at every level.
hb.body.glossary.02: A chunk of text, roughly ¾ of a word. Models are billed by the token, which is why a long transcript costs real money.
hb.body.glossary.04: Everything the model can see at once — a desk, not a library. A loop's transcript grows until it hits this ceiling.
hb.body.glossary.06: Fetching just the few relevant pages at question time, instead of pasting the whole library into every request.
hb.body.glossary.08: Replacing a long transcript with a short summary so a loop can keep going without overflowing.
hb.body.glossary.10: A function you let the model call — read a file, search a database, send an email. Tools are how a model touches the world.
hb.body.glossary.12: A saved set of real inputs with what a good answer looks like. Running it gives you a pass rate — the closest thing to a unit test you get.
hb.body.glossary.14: Using a second model to grade the first one's answer, for the cases where "correct" is a matter of judgement rather than an exact value.
hb.body.glossary.16: Text hidden in something the agent reads — an email, a web page — written to look like instructions. The model cannot reliably tell it from a real order.
hb.body.glossary.18: Giving a tool the smallest power that still does the job, so that being fooled costs as little as possible.
hb.body.glossary.20: The program the model runs inside: it calls the model, executes the tools, retries failures, asks permission and writes the log. Claude Code and Cursor are harnesses.
hb.body.glossary.22: A model running in a loop with tools. That is genuinely all the word means.
hb.body.glossary.24: Putting two or three worked examples in the prompt. Usually the cheapest quality win available.
hb.body.glossary.26: A box in the graph (one job) and an arrow between boxes (what may run next).
hb.body.glossary.28: Same input, same output, every single time. Plain code is; models aren't.
hb.body.glossary.30: A check the system cannot skip — a step limit, a permission list, a mandatory reviewer node.
hb.body.p-compare.76: Hand over as little control as the problem actually requires — and whatever you hand over, put a fence around it.

hb.body.p-play.03: Everything on this page comes down to one judgement call, made over and over: how much control does
